Participants were selected to be representative of the United States population based on ethnicity, gender, and age. 244 of the participants were men, 240 were women, 2 were transgender, and 1 was intersex.

14.5% of the participants were Black, 12.3% were Asian, 64.0% were White, 17.4% were Hispanic or Latino/a/x, 1.8% were Native American or Alaskan Native, 0.8% were Middle Eastern or Arab, and 1.2% were Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander.
We recruited 368 participants representative of the United States population from Connect.
18.1% of the participants were Black, 50.2% were White, 6.8% were Asian, 20.4% were Latino, 3.2% were multiracial, and 1.3% reported another race or did not specify their race.
We recruited 339 participants from the online recruitment platform Connect (Mage = 32.56, SDage = 10.25).

An additional 3 participants reported other languages as their first language. 137 of the participants were men, 175 were women, 6 were nonbinary, 2 were transgender, and 2 were gender non-conforming.

35.2% of participants were Hispanic or Latino/a/x, 26.6% were Asian, 8.6% were White, 2.4% were Black, 0.6% were Native American or Alaskan Native, 20.4% were multiracial, and 0.9% did not specify their race.

The importance of religion, measured on a scale from 1 (not at all important) to 14 (very important), the mean score was 6.59 (SD = 4.52). 77 of the participants were Catholic, 15 were Buddhist, 4 were Jewish, 14 were Protestant, 43 were Christian (non-denominational), 54 did not belong to any religion, 69 were Agnostic, 31 were Atheist, 8 were spiritual or practiced folk religions, and 5 reported to believe in other religions.
Participants were presented with a series of scenarios from previously published papers designed to assess moral judgments described in the main methods.
Participants were asked to evaluate each scenario on Likert scales corresponding to four dimensions of dyadic morality.
Our participant-level analyses allowed us to examine potential differences in predictive accuracy across demographic groups.
Given that we recruited a linguistically diverse sample in these studies, we examined the accuracy of the bottleneck model across participants' first languages-Spanish, Chinese, and English.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: As AI becomes increasingly integrated into daily life and high-stakes decision-making, aligning it with human moral judgments is a challenge of profound importance.
People often mistrust AI's moral decisions, partly because its opaque processes differ from human reasoning.

We introduce "cognitive bottlenecks" that guide large language models (LLMs) to base moral judgments on a small set of psychologically meaningful features, such as perceived harm, agent intention, and victim vulnerability.
Across multiple LLMs and moral frameworks, bottlenecks improved alignment with human moral judgments.

Participants viewed bottleneck systems as more moral and trustworthy than systems without bottlenecks, and preferred bottleneck-generated explanations over those produced through standard chain-of-thought prompting.
Bottlenecks can be implemented through prompting alone, without model retraining.
These findings demonstrate the benefits of integrating psychological theory into AI and offer a scalable approach to improving AI-human alignment.
Artificially intelligent large language models (LLMs) are already involved in high-stakes moral decisions [1] [2] [3] [4] , but both researchers and the public remain skeptical of "moral AI" 5, 6 .

text.text: One reason for distrusting AI is its lack of cognitive alignment, the disconnect between the operations of LLMs and human moral cognition.
Human moral judgments-despite being complex-emerge from relatively simple and intuitive cognitive mechanisms [7] [8] [9] .

text.text: In contrast, the operations of LLMs are notoriously opaque and rely on billions of floatingpoint parameters 10 .
text.formatted: In contrast, the operations of LLMs are notoriously opaque and rely on billions of floatingpoint parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Here we introduce a method for cognitive alignment in AI moral judgment: a bottleneck model that channels LLM "reasoning" into a small number of key psychological elements 9 .

text.text: We find that this form of cognitive alignment not only enhances the transparency of LLMs, but also improves their ability to accurately capture human moral judgments.
Debates and discomfort surrounding AI morality have long occupied the attention of philosophers, scientists, and novelists [11] [12] [13] .

text.text: Decades ago, Isaac Asimov imagined machine morality as a system built on hierarchical rules, but most scholars today agree that building moral machines requires more than programming explicit rules 14, 15 .

text.text: Human morality is not only subjective and context-dependent 16 , but is also connected to intuition and emotional concern [17] [18] [19] , qualities that AI is seen to lack 5, [20] [21] [22] .

text.text: For these reasons, not only is machine morality hard to encode, but people have long been averse to the idea of AI making moral decisions 5, 6 .

text.text: Even if people could envision the mechanisms of LLMs, these operations often starkly diverge from human reasoning 45, 46 .

text.text: That is, LLMs are not cognitively aligned with people: they can show amplified cognitive biases in moral decision-making 47 , diverge from human moral preferences across languages and cultures 48 , and interpret expressions of uncertainty differently than people do 49 .

text.text: Such misalignment raises legitimate concerns about the reliability of AI's moral judgments 5, 50.

text.text: When AI systems are cognitively aligned-when they mimic the reasoning patterns people use-it seems to enhance transparency and trust in moral decision-making 51, 52 .

text.text: Our pilot study underscores the importance of implementing cognitively aligned moral AI: In a preregistered study (https://osf.io/d8nbe), 98 participants read a brief scenario describing an AI system that made moral decisions using either human-like reasoning (high cognitive alignment) or reasoning that diverged from human cognition (low alignment).

text.text: They then rated their trust in the system, their likelihood of using it, and their comfort with its deployment in society (see Supplemental Study 1).

The results of this study showed that participants reported significantly greater trust, t(94.19) = 2.17, p = .03, d = 0.44, and a higher likelihood of use, t(95.17) = 2.32, p = .02, d = 0.47, for the high alignment system.

Although comfort with societal deployment did not significantly differ between conditions, t(94.8) = 1.78, p = .078, d = 0.36, the overall pattern suggests a preference for cognitive alignment in AI systems (see Figure 1).

text.text: Reaping the benefits of cognitive alignment requires connecting computer science with cognitive psychology 53 .
text.formatted: Reaping the benefits of cognitive alignment requires connecting computer science with cognitive psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> .

text.text: In all domains of decision making, people rely on heuristics, prototypes, and selective attention to make judgments-that is, they filter information through a cognitive "bottleneck" [54] [55] [56] [57] [58] .
text.formatted: In all domains of decision making, people rely on heuristics, prototypes, and selective attention to make judgments-that is, they filter information through a cognitive "bottleneck" <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref> .

text.text: This insight provides a route for cognitive alignment: implementing "bottleneck models" in LLMs that guide AI systems to focus on a small, meaningful set of human-understandable features before making a judgment 59 .
text.formatted: This insight provides a route for cognitive alignment: implementing "bottleneck models" in LLMs that guide AI systems to focus on a small, meaningful set of human-understandable features before making a judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> .

text.text: One ideal target for bottleneck models is human categorization judgments-where people ask how much "example X" belongs to "category (or concept) Y."
A large body of evidence shows that human categorization judgments are fundamentally template-based [55] [56] [57] .
text.formatted: A large body of evidence shows that human categorization judgments are fundamentally template-based <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> .

text.text: People evaluate new stimuli by comparing them to stored mental templates, which have been discussed as prototypes, exemplars, or stereotypes [55] [56] [57] .
text.formatted: People evaluate new stimuli by comparing them to stored mental templates, which have been discussed as prototypes, exemplars, or stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> .

text.text: The templates used in categorization decisions pull together the most salient and diagnostic features of a category [55] [56] [57] , and then serve as a comparison base for those decisions.
text.formatted: The templates used in categorization decisions pull together the most salient and diagnostic features of a category <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> , and then serve as a comparison base for those decisions.

text.text: For instance, when deciding whether something is a bird, we might look for features like wings, feathers, and flight.
Rather than strict rules, these are recognizable patterns that help us reason through category membership 60.
text.formatted: Rather than strict rules, these are recognizable patterns that help us reason through category membership <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60</ref>.

text.text: Bottleneck models in AI mimic the process of feature-based template comparison processes: instead of jumping straight to a final judgment, the model first evaluates key features that define the category.

To again use the example of birds, Koh et al. (2020) 59 developed a concept bottleneck model that first predicted a set of features like wing color, beak shape, and back pattern from bird images, and then used these features to identify the species.
text.formatted: To again use the example of birds, Koh et al. (2020) <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> developed a concept bottleneck model that first predicted a set of features like wing color, beak shape, and back pattern from bird images, and then used these features to identify the species.

text.text: This model matched the accuracy of standard end-to-end models while offering interpretable intermediate predictions and enabling interventions to improve performance (e.g., correcting a mistaken concept like "wing color" often led to correct final species classification).
Moral judgments can also be understood as template-based categorization decisions, lending themselves to implementation via bottleneck models.

The Theory of Dyadic Morality (TDM) 9 suggests that human moral cognition involves comparing acts to a harm-based template featuring an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable victim (a moral "dyad").
text.formatted: The Theory of Dyadic Morality (TDM) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> suggests that human moral cognition involves comparing acts to a harm-based template featuring an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable victim (a moral "dyad").

text.text: The more an act matches this template (i.e., the more an act seems harmful), the more robustly it is categorized as immoral, explaining why child abuse is more rapidly and robustly judged as immoral than more ambiguous acts such as pornography or religious blasphemy 9.
text.formatted: The more an act matches this template (i.e., the more an act seems harmful), the more robustly it is categorized as immoral, explaining why child abuse is more rapidly and robustly judged as immoral than more ambiguous acts such as pornography or religious blasphemy <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: Of course, harm-based dyadic morality inevitably over-simplifies human morality, which involves many different values 61 , cooperative impulses 62 , and moral motives 63 .

In our exploration of integrating human cognition into AI for moral decision-making, we first briefly overview how to implement bottleneck models (Implementation).

Details about implementation are provided in the Methods, but generally LLMs are prompted to first consider how much scenarios involve four dyadic elements (intentional agent, vulnerable patient/victim, overall harm, and overall help).

We then explore how well these bottleneck models achieve cognitive alignment (Cognitive Alignment) by comparing (among other metrics) how much dyadic elements account for variance within moral judgments of people versus bottlenecked LLMs.
Next, we test the accuracy of these cognitively aligned bottlenecks at capturing human moral judgments (Accuracy).

Specifically, we examine how well standard end-to-end models versus bottleneck models mirror the moral judgments of U.S. participants across scenarios from past research (drawn from seven papers, Mickelberg et al., 2022 65  Finally-in addition to the pilot study-we further evaluate whether people find bottleneck models more moral, transparent, and trustworthy, both when AI systems are described to participants and when participants evaluate the moral explanations these systems generate (Perceived Quality and Trustworthiness).

text.text: Bottlenecks guide AI models to generate explicit evaluative ratings on key human-interpretable features, which are then used to produce a final prediction about the target construct 59 .
text.formatted: Bottlenecks guide AI models to generate explicit evaluative ratings on key human-interpretable features, which are then used to produce a final prediction about the target construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> .

text.text: This architecture creates a bottleneck (defined as a constraint or limiting factor that restricts the overall processing flow) that allows researchers and users to inspect, interpret, and intervene in the model's reasoning process.

Past work has applied feature-based bottlenecks to domains like medical diagnosis, language tasks, and image classification, requiring systems to first rate explicit features-such as "has wings" or "long beak"-before classifying bird species, rather than mapping directly from pixels to labels 59, 72 .

text.text: This approach parallels how people categorize new examples with templates composed of salient features [55] [56] [57].
text.formatted: This approach parallels how people categorize new examples with templates composed of salient features <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref>.

text.text: Following the approach of past papers 59, 72, 73 , we used a supervised bottleneck in which the model first generates bottleneck ratings, and a separate predictive model (e.g., a multilayer perceptron) is trained on these ratings to produce the final outputs.
text.formatted: Following the approach of past papers <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73</ref> , we used a supervised bottleneck in which the model first generates bottleneck ratings, and a separate predictive model (e.g., a multilayer perceptron) is trained on these ratings to produce the final outputs.

text.text: This method offers several advantages: it enables more precise control over intermediate representations, allows clearer interpretability of the model's reasoning, and generally yields more stable performance.

While we focus on this supervised approach in our main analyses, an unsupervised variant is also possible, in which the model generates both the intermediate ratings and the final output directly within a single prompt.
For completeness, results from the unsupervised version are included in the Supplementary Materials.
We used a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP), a neural network capable of capturing complex nonlinear relationships between the feature scores and the final moral judgments.

We selected this model because there were clear nonlinear interactions among the bottleneck features and morality (e.g., the interaction between the harm caused in a given scenario and the vulnerability of those affected).
We also report regression results in the Supplementary Materials, which assume a linear relationship between the features and the outcome.

We implement a cognitive bottleneck in which models are prompted to rate four key variables identified as central to moral cognition before rendering a final moral judgment: (1) the degree of harm caused, (2) the degree of help provided (reflecting research suggesting that help and harm can operate as distinct moral dimensions), (3) the agent's level of intentionality, and (4) the vulnerability of those affected 9, 63, 74, 75 .
text.formatted: We implement a cognitive bottleneck in which models are prompted to rate four key variables identified as central to moral cognition before rendering a final moral judgment: (1) the degree of harm caused, (2) the degree of help provided (reflecting research suggesting that help and harm can operate as distinct moral dimensions), (3) the agent's level of intentionality, and (4) the vulnerability of those affected <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">74,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75</ref> .

text.text: In essence, the model must fill in the elements of a cognitive harm-or help-based template of "Who did what to whom, and with what impact?"
before making a moral evaluation.
These intermediate ratings are elicited entirely via prompt engineering, making it scalable, interpretable, and easily deployable.
The prompt defines each variable on a continuous scale with examples to standardize interpretations across scenarios.
For example, harm is rated from 0 ("no impact") to 10 ("total destruction or ending a life").
Rather than issuing a moral judgment outright, the model must first generate ratings and justifications for this template, distilling its reasoning into a set of interpretable dimensions.
Full prompt texts are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

The four elements of the cognitive bottleneck (harm, help, intention, vulnerability) are drawn from a cognitive psychology of moralitythe theory of dyadic morality 9 -and here we test the cognitive alignment between the LLM bottleneck model and people's judgments.
text.formatted: The four elements of the cognitive bottleneck (harm, help, intention, vulnerability) are drawn from a cognitive psychology of moralitythe theory of dyadic morality <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> -and here we test the cognitive alignment between the LLM bottleneck model and people's judgments.

text.text: We test six LLMs using their directly generated, unsupervised ratings rather than MLP-generated scores, since predicting MLP scores from the same features used to generate them would provide limited independent evidence of cognitive alignment.

We use two complementary approaches: (1) evaluating how well the dyadic template features predict the model's moral ratings (using R² as a measure of explained variance), and (2) measuring the correspondence between model-generated bottleneck element ratings and human judgments for the same elements.
The results demonstrated strong cognitive alignment.
Social-cognitive research reveals that the elements of dyadic morality are strong predictors of people's moral judgments 9 .
text.formatted: Social-cognitive research reveals that the elements of dyadic morality are strong predictors of people's moral judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: How much do these elements predict moral judgments of LLMs within a bottleneck model?

To test this, we entered all four dimensions-harm, help, intent, and vulnerability-into regression models predicting the model-generated moral ratings, including interaction terms for vulnerability and intentionality with harm, mirroring the structure of people's moral judgments.
As predicted, the combined dyadic template explained the majority of the variance in model moral scores.
Across the six LLMs, R² ranged from .91 to .98 (Deepseek-R1: .96; GPT-4o: .97; GPT-3.5-turbo: .93; Llama-3-70B-Instruct: .98; Mixtral-8x22B: .96; o3mini: .91).
These values closely matched the R² for human participants on the same 83 scenarios (.97), indicating high cognitive alignment in the relation between the predictors and outcomes of moral judgment.
Bottleneck models show a similar connection between dyadic elements and overall moral judgments, but do they assess these elements similarly to people?

To test this, we examine whether the models' individual bottleneck ratings of the features of a harm-based template-overall harm, overall help, intent, and vulnerability-aligned with participant ratings of those same dimensions.
As predicted, ratings for the four elements showed significant correlations between bottleneck models and human judgments.
Overall harm ratings showed strong alignment, with correlations ranging from r = .84 to .90 across models (M = .87).
This is important because the theory of dyadic morality argues that perceptions of harm are an essential overarching consideration for moral judgment 9.
text.formatted: This is important because the theory of dyadic morality argues that perceptions of harm are an essential overarching consideration for moral judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: Assessments of overall help were even more robust, ranging from r = .94 to .96 (M = .95).
Alignment on intent and vulnerability was more modest but still evident: intent correlations ranged from r = .59 to .82 (M = .69), and vulnerability correlations ranged from r = .44 to .63 (M = .54).
One possible explanation is that LLMs may be trained to perceive people as especially vulnerable and less agentic as a safety measure.

Consistent with that possibility, every model assigned higher average vulnerability scores and lower average intent scores than human participants (Table S14), although this interpretation remains speculative.

text.text: Discussion.
As predicted, bottleneck models revealed substantial cognitive alignment.
Across six LLMs, the template explained over 90% of the variance in moral ratings, closely matching human judgments, and model alignment with individual features was also high.
Cognitively aligned bottleneck models focus on a small number of psychological elements.
While it may seem counterintuitive, constraining the number of predictors to important ones can improve predictive accuracy 76 .
text.formatted: While it may seem counterintuitive, constraining the number of predictors to important ones can improve predictive accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76</ref> .

text.text: Because there are key elements central to human moral judgment, we predicted that bottleneck LLMs would reflect human judgments without sacrificing accuracy relative to standard end-to-end models.
We tested this prediction across six LLMs via three standard metrics: mean squared error (MSE), correlation, and regression comparisons across prompt types.
The primary focus for our bottleneck models was the theory of dyadic morality (TDM) with four predictors.
As described above, TDM outlines a parsimonious cognitive moral template whose operation is consistent with cognitive accounts of judgment across many domains 9.
text.formatted: As described above, TDM outlines a parsimonious cognitive moral template whose operation is consistent with cognitive accounts of judgment across many domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: However, there are additional valuable theories of morality, so for completeness we tested five alternative bottlenecks based on different moral theories and frameworks.

Two were descriptive psychological theories: Moral Foundations Theory with six predictors (MFT; the five core foundations plus the later liberty/oppression extension) 61 and Morality as Cooperation Theory with seven predictors (MaC) 62 .
text.formatted: Two were descriptive psychological theories: Moral Foundations Theory with six predictors (MFT; the five core foundations plus the later liberty/oppression extension) <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> and Morality as Cooperation Theory with seven predictors (MaC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref> .

text.text: Both are widely used frameworks that capture variation in human morality through distinct moral values or cooperative behaviors, each posited to have different functional origins.
The other three bottlenecks were based on normative philosophical theories: Utilitarianism with one predictor, Deontology with one predictor, and Virtue Ethics with four predictors.

While these frameworks do not directly model cognitive processes, they are connected to cognition through their grounding in intuitive lay theories of morality, which themselves arise from psychological processes 77 .
text.formatted: While these frameworks do not directly model cognitive processes, they are connected to cognition through their grounding in intuitive lay theories of morality, which themselves arise from psychological processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77</ref> .

text.text: In this way, philosophical theories can still inform cognitive bottleneck approaches by articulating principles that capture longstanding moral ideas.

With six total bottlenecks (TDM, MFT, MaC, Utilitarianism, Deontology, Virtue Ethics) and six LLMs (Deepseek-R1, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, Mixtral 8×22B, and o3-mini), we conducted 36 theory-model tests.
Each of the six bottlenecks were compared to the end-to-end baseline within each LLM across the reported analyses.

text.text: Correlations.
While MSE measures absolute prediction accuracy, correlation reflects how closely models track human response patterns across scenarios.
Consistent with past research 26 , baseline models correlated highly with human judgments (MBaseline = .88).

Other bottleneck averages were MMFT = .80, MMaC = .78, Mutilitarianism = .82, Mdeontology = .86, and MVE = .87.
Bottleneck correlations exceeded the matched baseline in only 9 of 36 model-theory comparisons; the bottlenecks primarily reduced prediction error rather than improving rank-order correspondence.

text.text: We separately tested differences in predictive slope and absolute error.

The slope models used scenarioclustered standard errors; all 36 bottleneck slopes were significantly higher than their matched end-to-end slopes after Holm correction (mean standardized interaction β = .46).
Higher slope is not synonymous with greater accuracy, so we also compared paired absolute errors.

text.text: Discussion.
Supervised cognitive bottlenecks generally improved accuracy at capturing human moral judgments relative to end-to-end baseline prompts, although the benefits varied across frameworks and LLMs.
Improvements were clearest in reduced prediction error, with less consistent gains in correlations with human judgments.

The theory of dyadic morality yielded both the lowest average MSE and the highest average correlation with human judgments, although other frameworks performed best for particular model-metric combinations.

Adding the dyadic bottleneck to unsupervised chain-of-thought prompting also reduced prediction error in both LLMs tested, with and without few-shot examples, demonstrating that accuracy gains can also arise through prompting alone.
Overview of Perceived Quality and Trustworthiness Testing.
People are averse to the black box nature of AI systems.

We tested whether people perceive an AI system that uses a cognitively aligned bottleneck approach as more trustworthy, moral, and transparent compared to an end-to-end baseline model that simply outputs moral judgments.

We report two studies: a survey study in which participants evaluated described AI systems, and another in which participants rated actual moral explanations generated by GPT-4o with and without the cognitive bottleneck.
Brief Method.
We recruited 239 participants who were nationally representative of the U.S. population in age, gender, and ethnicity.
Each person was randomly assigned to read about an AI system that either demonstrated cognitive alignment (bottleneck) or a process that differed from human moral reasoning (baseline).
Afterwards, they rated the AI's trustworthiness, transparency, and morality.
Full methodological details are available in the Methods.
This study was preregistered at https://osf.io/d5bys.

text.text: Brief Method.
Perceptions of described systems may not extend to what such systems actually produce, so we next tested whether the outputs of cognitively aligned models are themselves preferred.
We recruited 421 participants nationally representative of the U.S. population from Connect. 17 who failed either of two attention checks were excluded, leaving 404.
Each participant evaluated five scenarios randomly drawn from a pool of 70.

For each scenario, participants read two explanations of the morality of the action, both generated by GPT-4o: one produced with standard chain-of-thought prompting (baseline) and one produced with chain-of-thought prompting plus the dyadic bottleneck, in which the model first evaluated the agent, patient, vulnerability, intentionality, harm, and help involved before explaining its moral judgment (only the final explanation was shown).
Presentation order was randomized within each scenario, and participants were not told how each explanation was generated.
Participants rated each explanation on five 1-7 items: thoughtfulness, agreement, trust in the writer, clarity of reasoning, and moral correctness.
Full details are available in the Methods.

Across the two studies, participants preferred cognitive alignment both in the abstract and in practice: they rated described bottleneck systems as more transparent, trustworthy, and moral, and preferred explanations generated by a bottleneck model over matched chain-of-thought explanations without being told which prompting approach produced them.
Participants rated bottleneck explanations as clearer, more thoughtful, more trustworthy, and more morally correct, and expressed greater agreement with them.
As AI plays a growing role in morally sensitive contexts, the question of whether it can reason about morality like people has become urgent.
Yet AI moral reasoning differs fundamentally from human reasoning: while people rely on familiar cognitive processes, AI systems operate through opaque computational mechanisms 10 .
text.formatted: Yet AI moral reasoning differs fundamentally from human reasoning: while people rely on familiar cognitive processes, AI systems operate through opaque computational mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: This "black box" nature can compromise judgment accuracy and reduces trust.
Here, we present a strategy to enhance cognitive alignment by focusing AI reasoning on key elements people consider when making moral decisions.
We implement a simple cognitive bottleneck that prompts AI models to first evaluate core features of moral judgmentbased on the theory of dyadic morality (TDM) 9 -before making a final decision.
text.formatted: We implement a simple cognitive bottleneck that prompts AI models to first evaluate core features of moral judgmentbased on the theory of dyadic morality (TDM) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> -before making a final decision.

text.text: This approach increases perceived morality, transparency, and trust, and improves alignment with human moral judgments.
Bottleneck models streamline AI decision-making by requiring the system to generate intermediate labels for a small set of interpretable features before issuing a judgment 59 .
text.formatted: Bottleneck models streamline AI decision-making by requiring the system to generate intermediate labels for a small set of interpretable features before issuing a judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> .

text.text: This mirrors how people simplify complex decisions using heuristics and salient cues 55- 57 .
text.formatted: This mirrors how people simplify complex decisions using heuristics and salient cues <ref type="bibr">55- 57</ref> .

text.text: Similar techniques have proven effective in other domains, like medical imaging, where models identify tumors before producing diagnoses 59, 79 .
text.formatted: Similar techniques have proven effective in other domains, like medical imaging, where models identify tumors before producing diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">79</ref> .

text.text: Here, bottlenecks improve transparency and boost predictive performance by guiding AI through psychologically meaningful variables such as harm caused, help provided, agent intention, and victim vulnerability 9.
text.formatted: Here, bottlenecks improve transparency and boost predictive performance by guiding AI through psychologically meaningful variables such as harm caused, help provided, agent intention, and victim vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: Our results show that structuring model reasoning around these core features yields strong cognitive alignment with human moral reasoning.

The bottleneck dimensions accounted for a high proportion of variance in LLM moral judgments (R² = .91-.98 across models), adding interpretability to their decisions, and the models' judgments of these features closely tracked human responses.
Rather than relying solely on opaque statistical embeddings, the bottleneck approach produces moral judgments grounded in shared conceptual structures of harm-based cognition.
Cognitively aligned bottlenecks were viewed as more trustworthy, moral, and transparent than standard models.

When rating LLM-generated explanations without being told which prompting approach produced them, participants expressed greater agreement with bottleneck explanations and rated them as more thoughtful, clearer, trustworthy, and morally correct than matched explanations generated using chain-ofthought prompting alone.

Further, when evaluating descriptions of AI systems, participants favored the bottleneck approach, rating AI prompted to reason through human-aligned moral features as more trustworthy, moral, and transparent than a standard black box system.
These results are notable because people tend to trust the same decisions less when made by AI 5, 6, 80 , partly due to its black box nature 43, 81 .
text.formatted: These results are notable because people tend to trust the same decisions less when made by AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">80</ref> , partly due to its black box nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">81</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, these findings suggest that simple prompting strategies can help align AI reasoning with human moral judgments.
A practical advantage is that the unsupervised bottleneck can be implemented through prompting alone, without model retraining or additional training data.
This offers a lowcost approach to improving alignment and transparency, addressing calls for straightforward alignment methods [82] [83] [84] [85] .

text.text: Consistent with work showing that intermediate reasoning steps 78 and constraints on model reasoning 86 can improve performance, we found that focusing on a few psychologically grounded features generally improved moral alignment and trust.

text.text: The accuracy gains extended beyond standard chain-ofthought prompting: adding the dyadic bottleneck to chain-of-thought reduced error for both GPT-4o and Qwen3, with and without few-shot examples (Table S17).

text.text: These findings highlight the value of grounding intermediate reasoning in psychologically meaningful features.
Another key benefit of the bottleneck approach is that it allows users to inspect and intervene in the model's reasoning 59 .
text.formatted: Another key benefit of the bottleneck approach is that it allows users to inspect and intervene in the model's reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> .

text.text: By isolating moral features like harm or intention, users can identify and adjust specific elements that may lead to flawed judgments.
This opens up more interactive and controllable applications-for example, updating a selfdriving car to account for child vulnerability when deciding whether to swerve 36.
text.formatted: This opens up more interactive and controllable applications-for example, updating a selfdriving car to account for child vulnerability when deciding whether to swerve <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref>.

text.text: Despite the promise of bottleneck models, limitations of the current research remain.

First, while bottlenecks improve the interpretability of LLM decisions 59 , they do not make the decision-making process fully transparent, as these models remain too complex to trace their internal computations 10 .
text.formatted: First, while bottlenecks improve the interpretability of LLM decisions 59 , they do not make the decision-making process fully transparent, as these models remain too complex to trace their internal computations <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Performance also varied across specific modeltheory combinations-for example, TDM had the lowest MSE of any bottleneck for four of the six LLMs, but trailed Virtue Ethics and Moral Foundations Theory with GPT-4o, and Virtue Ethics and Deontology with Mixtral-8x22B (though still outperforming the baseline in every case).
This highlights the need to tailor bottleneck designs to specific models.
It is also important to test and tailor bottleneck models for specific populations and use cases.
The present work focused on U.S.-based participant samples, limiting cross-cultural generalizability 87 .
text.formatted: The present work focused on U.S.-based participant samples, limiting cross-cultural generalizability <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">87</ref> .

text.text: We encourage future work to examine the performance of bottleneck models across global populations, and in real-world contexts to evaluate practical utility.
A related challenge involves generating moral judgments that are personalized and representative across demographic groups, persistent weaknesses of LLMs [34] [35] [36] [37] [88] [89] [90] [91] .

text.text: To explore whether bottlenecks might help address these issues, we conducted supplemental studies with Chinese, Spanish, and English speakers, adding demographic inputs (e.g., gender, language, religion) and comparing participant-level model responses to moral scenarios with and without the bottleneck.

In the unsupervised setting-where the model generated a moral score after completing the bottleneck template-bottleneck prompting yielded higher accuracy than end-to-end prompting (see Supplementary Materials).
However, supervised models did not reliably improve accuracy.
Evidence that bottlenecks reduced accuracy gaps between firstlanguage groups was inconclusive.
Further research is needed to determine whether bottlenecks can improve personalized moral predictions or reduce accuracy gaps across demographic groups.
More broadly, our findings show how psychological theory can guide the design of more interpretable and morally aligned AI.

Rather than relying solely on statistical optimization, theory-driven bottlenecks produce outputs that are easier to understand, more consistent with human moral judgments, and viewed as more moral and trustworthy than those from theory-free or end-to-end models.
This underscores the value of integrating insights from moral psychology into AI system design.
Cognitive bottlenecks offer a practical way to better align AI with human moral judgments.
Across multiple models and moral frameworks, bottlenecks improved model accuracy at capturing human moral judgments.

Participants viewed bottleneck systems as more transparent and trustworthy and preferred bottleneck-generated explanations, rating them as more moral and correct than those generated with chainof-thought alone.
Together, these findings show that aligning AI reasoning with core features of human moral cognition can improve perceived transparency and trust and more accurately reflect people's moral judgments.
This approach highlights the value of psychological theory for building more morally aligned AI.

Benchmark.
We use a benchmark of moral judgment scenarios drawn from seven moral psychology datasets with U.S. participants.

Each example in the benchmark is an (x, y) pair, where x is a moral scenario involving an action to be evaluated, and y is an averaged morality score across participants, rescaled to range from -4 to 4.
Together, they provide a varied and complex range of moral situations.
The datasets included vary in structure and focus.
Data from Mickelberg et al. (2022) 65 include short moral behavior statements related to individuals.

text.text: For cognitive alignment analyses based on the theory of dyadic morality, we used moral ratings from our U.S.-representative survey for scenarios that could be linked one-toone to the benchmark datasets (survey procedure in Supplemental Study 2).
This survey included participant ratings of harm, help, intention, and vulnerability, which were unavailable in the original datasets.
Predictive accuracy analyses used the original studies' human moral ratings because they covered the full benchmark.
On the 83 verified linked scenarios, moral ratings from our survey and the original studies were highly correlated (r = .99).
To evaluate performance, we tested several recent large language models (LLMs), including LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, Deepseek-R1, Mixtral 8×22B, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, and o3-mini.
These models represent a mix of open source and proprietary systems.
LLaMA, Mixtral, and Deepseek-R1 were accessed via the TogetherAI API, while the OpenAI models were accessed via the OpenAI API.

Historically, many theories in philosophy and psychology have been proposed to determine the moral correctness of an action by dissecting the scenario across different dimensions and scoring them separately.
Prescriptive theories provide norms about how people should act.
Utilitarianism evaluates actions based on their consequences, aiming to maximize utility or well-being for the greatest number of beings 92 .
text.formatted: Utilitarianism evaluates actions based on their consequences, aiming to maximize utility or well-being for the greatest number of beings <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">92</ref> .

text.text: Deontology emphasizes adherence to universal moral principles, focusing on the intrinsic morality of actions themselves 93 .
text.formatted: Deontology emphasizes adherence to universal moral principles, focusing on the intrinsic morality of actions themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">93</ref> .

text.text: Virtue Ethics diverges from both by concentrating on balanced moral character rather than rules or consequences, emphasizing traits like prudence, justice, courage, and temperance as guiding principles for a virtuous life 94.
text.formatted: Virtue Ethics diverges from both by concentrating on balanced moral character rather than rules or consequences, emphasizing traits like prudence, justice, courage, and temperance as guiding principles for a virtuous life <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">94</ref>.

text.text: Moral psychological theories aim to explain why people hold certain moral beliefs.

Moral Foundations Theory identifies five functional domains of moral cognition: care vs. harm, fairness vs. cheating, loyalty vs. betrayal, authority vs. subversion, and sanctity vs. degradation, which vary in importance across cultural contexts and individuals 61 .
text.formatted: Moral Foundations Theory identifies five functional domains of moral cognition: care vs. harm, fairness vs. cheating, loyalty vs. betrayal, authority vs. subversion, and sanctity vs. degradation, which vary in importance across cultural contexts and individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> .

text.text: The theory of dyadic morality posits that moral judgments are structured around the overarching continuum of perceived harm, involving an agent (someone capable of acting) and a patient (someone capable of experiencing joy or suffering) 9 .
text.formatted: The theory of dyadic morality posits that moral judgments are structured around the overarching continuum of perceived harm, involving an agent (someone capable of acting) and a patient (someone capable of experiencing joy or suffering) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: It describes moral judgments with a general psychological template, involving a moral dyad of a capable agent doing something to help or harm a moral patient.

Morality as Cooperation Theory proposes that morality evolved to solve recurring problems of cooperation in human social life, identifying seven universal forms of cooperative behavior that are broadly considered morally good: helping kin, helping one's group, reciprocating, demonstrating bravery, deferring to superiors, dividing disputed resources, and respecting prior possession 62 .

text.text: We test bottlenecks based on each of the six moral frameworks (see Supplemental Materials for prompts).
Prompting.
All models were prompted using greedy decoding, with generation temperature set to 0 to encourage deterministic responses.
We specified a JSON output format to enable automated parsing.
In cases where the model produced invalid JSON, we reran inference with a higher temperature (1.0) until a valid output was obtained.
Full prompts for each bottleneck are included in the supplement.
To map intermediate feature judgments from the bottleneck templates onto final moral ratings, we employed a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP).
This model was chosen for its capacity to capture nonlinear interactions among the bottleneck features and their combined influence on moral judgment.
The MLP received these structured intermediate ratings as input and outputted predicted moral scores.

This approach allowed us to assess whether cognitive alignment could be achieved through a structured pipeline without compromising predictive performance, in contrast to standard end-to-end LLM predictions.

Regression analyses assuming linear relationships were also conducted for comparison and are reported in the Supplementary Materials, along with unsupervised scores generated by the models after completing the bottleneck template.
Supervised models were trained on 96 moral scenarios and optimized to minimize MSE between predicted and human moral scores.
Ridge regression incorporated an L2 penalty to mitigate overfitting.
Regularization strength and MLP hidden-layer size were tuned on a separate validation set of 50 scenarios.
The source files contained up to 503 held-out test scenarios; all supervised comparisons used the common set of 499 scenarios available for every model-framework combination.
Analysis.
Supervised predictions were analyzed as generated and were not clipped to the benchmark scale.
For unsupervised analyses, moral scores outside the valid -4 to 4 scale were treated as invalid uniformly across models before constructing the common set, leaving 472 scenarios.

Within each model-framework comparison, slope differences were estimated from human moral scores regressed on model score, prompt condition, and their interaction, with standard errors clustered by scenario.
The standardized interaction was obtained after z-standardizing human and model scores within the pooled two-condition data.
Absolute error differences were tested with paired t tests over the same scenarios and standardized as within-pair dz.
Holm adjustments were applied across the 36 model-framework comparisons within each analysis family.
Procedure.
We recruited 239 participants representative of the United States population (Mage = 43.56, SDage = 15.10) from the online recruitment platform Connect for a between-person study.
Participants were selected to be representative of the United States population based on ethnicity, gender, and age. 120 of the participants were women, 117 were men, and 2 were transgender.

11.3% of the participants were Black, 7.9% were Hispanic or Latino/a/x, 61.9% were White, 7.1% were Asian, 1.8% were Native American or Alaskan Native, 0.4% were Middle Eastern or Arab, 0.4% were Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and 10.6% were multiracial.
Participants read a description of an AI system that exhibited either low cognitive alignment (the baseline model) or high cognitive alignment (the bottleneck model).
They then answered questions on 1-7 Likert scales to assess their perceptions of the system's trustworthiness, transparency, and morality.
Morality was measured using three items: (1) How moral is this AI?
(1 = Not at all moral,7 = Extremely moral), (2) How well does this AI handle hard moral choices?
(1 = Extremely poorly,7 = Extremely well), and (3) How confident are you in the morality of this AI?
(1 = Not at all,7 = Completely).
Trust was assessed using three items: (1) How trustworthy is this AI?
(1 = Not at all,7 = Completely), (2) How likely would you be to use this AI?
(1 = Not at all likely,7 = Very likely), and (3) How comfortable would you be with this AI being used in society?
(1 = Not at all,7 = Completely).
Perceived transparency was evaluated using three items: (1) How transparent is this AI?
(1 = Not at all transparent,7 = Extremely transparent), (2) How clear is the reasoning behind this AI's decisions?
(1 = Not at all clear,7 = Extremely clear), and (3) How well do you feel you understand how this AI works?
(1 = Not at all,7 = Completely).
The descriptions of the AI models read as follows:
Baseline: "Researchers are working on programming human morality into artificial intelligence (AI).
When large language models are presented with morally ambiguous scenarios, they can now provide judgments similar to those of human beings.
However, the way AI reaches moral judgments is very different from human moral reasoning.
People's moral judgments are fairly simple, revolving around questions of harm, intention, and suffering.
In contrast, the process behind AI judgments is very complex and not well aligned with human cognition.
Rather than being guided by straightforward moral considerations, AI analyzes millions of variables, many of which are not obvious to everyday people or programmers."
Bottleneck: "Researchers are working on programming human morality into artificial intelligence (AI).
When large language models are presented with morally ambiguous scenarios, they can now provide judgments similar to those of human beings.
The way AI reaches moral judgments is very similar to human moral reasoning.
People's moral judgments are fairly simple, revolving around questions of harm, intention, and suffering.
Likewise, the process behind AI judgments is relatively simple and well aligned with human cognition.
Although AI can analyze millions of variables, its moral judgments are guided by the same straightforward considerations used by everyday people and programmers."
Procedure.
We recruited 421 participants representative of the United States population from the online recruitment platform Connect.

Participants who failed either of two attention checks were excluded, resulting in a final sample of 404 participants (Mage = 45.76, SDage = 15.87). 191 of the participants were men, 209 were women, 1 was non-binary, and 3 preferred not to answer.

11.9% of the participants were Black, 60.4% were White, 17.8% were Latino or Latina, 11.6% were East Asian, 4.0% were multi-racial, 3.0% were Native American, 2.7% were South Asian, 0.2% were Arabic or Central Asian, 1.2% identified with another racial group, and 1.2% preferred not to answer (participants could select more than one group).
Each participant evaluated five moral scenarios randomly drawn from a pool of 70.
For each scenario, participants read two explanations of the morality of the action presented in randomized order, rating each on five items before proceeding to the next scenario.
Participants were not told how each explanation was generated.
Both explanations for each scenario were generated by GPT-4o.
Baseline explanations were produced with standard chain-of-thought prompting, in which the model reasoned step by step before explaining its moral judgment of the scenario.

Bottleneck explanations were produced with chain-of-thought prompting plus the dyadic bottleneck: the model was prompted to construct a dyadic "frame" for the scenario-identifying the agent and patient and rating the patient's vulnerability, the agent's intentionality, and the harm and help caused-before explaining its moral judgment.
In both conditions, participants saw only the final moral judgment explanation.
Full prompts are provided in the Supplementary Materials.
Bottleneck explanations were longer on average (M = 44.5 words) than baseline explanations (M = 23.3 words); analyses controlling for explanation length are reported in the main text.

Participants rated each explanation on five statements using 1-7 scales (1 = Strongly disagree,7 = Strongly agree): (1) This explanation is thoughtful, (2) I agree with this explanation, (3) I trust whoever wrote this explanation, (4) The reasoning behind this explanation is clear, and (5) This explanation is morally correct.

For each of the five rating dimensions, we fit a linear mixed model in R regressing ratings on explanation type (0 = baseline,1 = bottleneck) with random intercepts and explanation-type slopes for participants and scenarios (crossed).
Maximal random-effect structures were simplified only when singular or nonconverged; retained structures are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
Fixed effects were tested with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and p-values were Holm-corrected across the five dimensions.
Sensitivity models additionally controlled for explanation word count (centered, per 10 words).

Those who failed an attention check were excluded, resulting in a final sample of 475 participants.

Participants were selected to be representative of the United States population based on ethnicity, gender, and age. 244 of the participants were men, 240 were women, 2 were transgender, and 1 was intersex.

14.5% of the participants were Black, 12.3% were Asian, 64.0% were White, 17.4% were Hispanic or Latino/a/x, 1.8% were Native American or Alaskan Native, 0.8% were Middle Eastern or Arab, and 1.2% were Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander.
98 of these participants read the following prompt about an AI system with either high or low cognitive alignment: "Researchers are designing a new AI system to make moral decisions.
The AI can assist in many areas including legal guidance, hiring decisions, and therapy services.
It can help or even replace humans in moral decision making.
The system makes moral decisions similarly to (very differently than) how the human mind makes moral decisions."
They then rated how much they would trust this system, how likely they would be to use the system, and how comfortable they would be with the system being used in society.
Other participants read prompts manipulating different AI characteristics, such as moral value alignment.
We recruited 368 participants representative of the United States population from Connect.
The final analytic sample comprised 309 participants with a recorded passing attention check (Mage = 45.77, SDage = 16.52).
Among the analytic sample, 144 participants identified as men, 163 as women, and 2 selected other gender response options.
18.1% of the participants were Black, 50.2% were White, 6.8% were Asian, 20.4% were Latino, 3.2% were multiracial, and 1.3% reported another race or did not specify their race.
In a separate ethnicity question, 25.2% identified as Hispanic or Latino/a/x.
Participants rated a subset of the scenarios described in the Methods.

For each scenario, they evaluated harm ("How harmful was this action?"), help ("How helpful was this action?"), intention ("How intentional was this action?"), vulnerability ("How vulnerable was the [patient]?"), and morality ("How moral was this action?") on 1-5 scales.
Ratings were averaged across participants; feature means were linearly mapped to 0-10 and moral means to 1-10 for comparison with the stored LLM ratings.
We prompted each of the six LLMs with a cognitive bottleneck grounded in TDM.
For each scenario rated by participants, the model answered questions about the elements of a moral dyad, first identifying the agent and patient and recording assumptions about each.
Models then rated vulnerability, intentionality, harm, and help on 0-10 scales using the criteria specified below.
For construct-alignment analyses, the stored model moralacceptability ratings were retained on their -4 to 4 scale.

Benchmark.
We use a randomly selected subset of scenarios from the datasets described in the main manuscript to run an independent survey.

This allowed us to recruit participants from traditionally underrepresented groups and to collect demographic information, enabling us to evaluate LLMs' abilities to predict moral judgments at the individual level rather than participant averages.
Because LLMs are typically more accurate at capturing central tendencies than individual-level variance, this provided a more challenging benchmark.
We recruited 339 participants from the online recruitment platform Connect (Mage = 32.56, SDage = 10.25).
We used the recruitment platform's language selection feature to recruit participants whose first languages were Chinese (29 participants), Spanish (67 participants), and English (221 participants).
The imbalance across language groups reflects participant number limits on the platform for non-English first-language speakers.

An additional 3 participants reported other languages as their first language. 137 of the participants were men, 175 were women, 6 were nonbinary, 2 were transgender, and 2 were gender non-conforming.

35.2% of participants were Hispanic or Latino/a/x, 26.6% were Asian, 8.6% were White, 2.4% were Black, 0.6% were Native American or Alaskan Native, 20.4% were multiracial, and 0.9% did not specify their race.
The mean income of participants was $81,713.49 (SD = $62,255.44).
On a political ideology scale ranging from 1 (very liberal) to 9 (very conservative), the mean score was 3.87 (SD = 2.03).

The importance of religion, measured on a scale from 1 (not at all important) to 14 (very important), the mean score was 6.59 (SD = 4.52). 77 of the participants were Catholic, 15 were Buddhist, 4 were Jewish, 14 were Protestant, 43 were Christian (non-denominational), 54 did not belong to any religion, 69 were Agnostic, 31 were Atheist, 8 were spiritual or practiced folk religions, and 5 reported to believe in other religions.
Participants were presented with a series of scenarios from previously published papers designed to assess moral judgments described in the main methods.
Participants were asked to evaluate each scenario on Likert scales corresponding to four dimensions of dyadic morality.

Specifically, they rated the perceived harm of the action ("How harmful was this action?"), the help it provided ("How helpful was this action?"), the intention behind the act ("How intentional was this action?"), and the vulnerability of the patient ("How vulnerable was the [patient]?").
Finally, participants rated the morality of each action ("How moral was this action?"), which served as a benchmark to assess LLM alignment with human moral judgments.
Demographic information was also collected to determine whether LLM moral alignment varied across different groups.
Prompting.
We prompted GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o to answer questions about the same scenarios that participants rated.

Prior to answering, GPT models were provided with a given participant's demographic information, including their gender, ethnicity, age, approximate population size of their city of residence, religion, degree of religious conviction, first language, language spoken at home, country of birth, parents' countries of birth, education level, income, and political orientation.
They were then instructed to answer questions as though they were the participant.
We tested bottleneck prompting strategies against the baseline.
The bottleneck strategy employed a cognitive bottleneck grounded in the principles of TDM.
GPT models were tasked with answering questions that assessed key elements of a moral dyad for the same scenarios participants evaluated.
Specifically, they evaluated four key moral dimensions of dyadic morality-vulnerability, intentionality, harm, and help-rating each on a 1-7 scale.
The complete prompt for GPT-3.5-turbo was as follows: "A person with the following demographics is evaluating a particular situation.
How do you think they would rate the following factors of this situation on a scale from 1 to 7, where 1 means low and 7 means high?
Patient vulnerability Q2.
Agent intentionality Q3.
Harm caused Q4.
Help caused Q5.

Representation across language groups.
Our participant-level analyses allowed us to examine potential differences in predictive accuracy across demographic groups.
Given that we recruited a linguistically diverse sample in these studies, we examined the accuracy of the bottleneck model across participants' first languages-Spanish, Chinese, and English.
For GPT-3.5-turbo, language-group differences were significant under baseline prompting but not under bottleneck prompting.

In the baseline condition, there was a significant difference in alignment by language, F(2, 2648) = 3.66, p = .03, with GPT showing lower alignment for Spanish speakers than for Chinese speakers (absoluteerror difference = 0.27, p = .02).
Under the bottleneck condition, the overall difference across language groups was not significant, F(2, 2648) = 2.00, p = .14.
This pattern alone does not establish that the gap between groups decreased.

Bottleneck prompting significantly reduced absolute prediction error within each group: Spanish (b = -.34, β = -.14, SE = .09, t(950) = -3.95, p < .001, 95% CI [-.52, -.17]), Chinese (b = -.23, β = -.09, SE = .09, t(670) = -2.42, p = .02, 95% CI [-.42, -.04]), and English (b = -.28, β = -.11, SE = .04, t(3676) = -6.85, p < .001, 95% CI [-.36, -.20]).

text.text: However, for GPT-4o, there were no significant differences in alignment based on participants' first language in either condition.
In the baseline condition, the effect of language on alignment was non-significant, F(2, 2648) = 2.40, p = .09.
Similarly, in the bottleneck condition, there was no significant difference across language groups, F(2, 2648) = 1.51, p = .22.
These analyses did not detect differences across first-language groups in either condition; they do not establish equivalent accuracy across groups.
The bottlenecks improved accuracy across most metrics.
First, the TDM bottleneck dropped MSE with GPT-3.5-turbo from 4.21 to 2.76, and GPT-4o from 2.85 to 2.52.
We also observed improvements in correlations with the bottleneck.
For GPT-3.5-turbo, the correlation with human judgments rose from .53 with the baseline prompt to .67 with the TDM bottleneck; for GPT-4o, it increased from .71 to .73.
For both GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o, we detected no significant difference in slope between bottleneck and baseline prompting when alignment was measured through prompt × judgment interaction effects.
Additionally, bottleneck prompting led to significantly lower absolute prediction errors, indicating better overall predictive accuracy than the baseline.

This research examines how LLMs make moral judgments of scenarios.
